papers.title: DT-Guard: Intent-Driven Reasoning-Active Training for Reasoning-Free LLM Safety Guardrail
papers.abstract: Large language models deployed in open-world applications require safety guardrails that are both robust to complex risks and efficient enough for low-latency runtime moderation. Existing guardrails face a practical trade-off between lightweight classification-based models, which are efficient but often struggle with concealed intent, ambiguous semantics, and borderline safety decisions, and reasoning-based guards, which improve judgment quality but introduce additional token generation and inference latency. We present DT-Guard, a content safety guardrail model based on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. The key idea is to use reasoning supervision during training while emitting only structured safety labels at inference time. DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process, Intent - Category - Safety, and constructs an intent-driven dataset with intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. To further improve hard-case robustness, we propose Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO), which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples, and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization accordingly. At inference time, DT-Guard directly generates structured labels without explicit reasoning traces, preserving deployment efficiency. Experiments on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks show that DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With only a 4B backbone, it reaches a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines. These results demonstrate that reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination.

summary.takeaway: DT-Guard internalizes reasoning supervision during training to achieve efficient, reasoning-free inference for robust LLM safety guardrails.
summary.problem: Existing LLM safety guardrails trade off between efficient but shallow classification and robust but slow reasoning-based methods.
summary.method: DT-Guard uses a progressive Intent → Category → Safety decision process with reasoning-active training and rollout-guided hard-case optimization, emitting only structured labels at inference.
summary.evidence: DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 on prompt-side and 0.870 on response-side benchmarks, outperforming 8B baselines with a 4B backbone.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of failure modes or generalization beyond tested benchmarks.
summary.why_for_you: DT-Guard offers a novel training paradigm that leverages reasoning supervision to improve adversarial robustness and efficiency in LLM safety guardrails.

signals.text: DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process: Intent recognition, risk Category attribution, and final Safety prediction, enabling clearer intermediate supervision for complex cases.

Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO) stratifies samples by multi-rollout consistency into mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable, applying targeted supervised fine-tuning and contrastive preference optimization.
Selective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training on borderline samples improves average F1 from 0.828 (full CoT) to 0.860, showing that uniform CoT supervision mismatches reasoning-free inference.

deep_dive.overview: DT-Guard addresses the challenge of deploying LLM safety guardrails that are both robust to complex, concealed intents and efficient for low-latency inference. Existing methods either rely on lightweight classification models that struggle with ambiguous or adversarial inputs or on reasoning-based models that incur high inference latency due to token generation of reasoning chains. DT-Guard introduces a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm, where explicit reasoning supervision is used only during training to internalize complex safety judgments. The model predicts structured safety labels through a progressive decision process: identifying user intent, attributing risk categories, and adjudicating safety levels. To enhance robustness on hard cases, DT-Guard employs RG-PHO, which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify sample difficulty and applies tailored supervised and preference-based optimization. Experiments on multiple prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks demonstrate that DT-Guard outperforms larger 8B parameter baselines with only a 4B backbone, achieving average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870 respectively, validating the effectiveness of reasoning supervision internalization for efficient safety discrimination.

methodology.title: Intent-Driven Progressive Safety Judgment
methodology.detail: Safety judgment is decomposed into a three-stage process: Intent recognition to capture underlying user motivation, Category attribution to assign relevant risk types, and Safety prediction to determine final safety labels. This structured approach provides intermediate supervision signals that improve robustness on ambiguous and borderline cases.

methodology.title: Reasoning-Active Training with Reasoning-Free Inference
methodology.detail: During training, DT-Guard uses explicit reasoning trajectories as supervision to guide the model in understanding complex safety decisions. At inference, the model emits only structured safety labels without generating reasoning chains, preserving low-latency deployment.

methodology.title: Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO)
methodology.detail: RG-PHO uses multiple model rollouts to assess sample consistency, stratifying samples into stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable. Persistently failed samples receive stronger supervised fine-tuning, while preference-unstable samples undergo contrastive preference optimization to stabilize judgments.

methodology.title: Selective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Supervision
methodology.detail: CoT reasoning supervision is selectively applied only to borderline samples rather than uniformly across all data, mitigating format mismatch with reasoning-free inference and improving overall F1 performance.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism equations provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes the progressive decision process and rollout consistency as conceptual mechanisms for improving safety judgment robustness.

experiments.title: Benchmark Evaluation on Prompt-Side and Response-Side Safety
experiments.detail: DT-Guard is evaluated on 10 prompt-side benchmarks (e.g., ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation, AegisSafety) and 7 response-side benchmarks (e.g., HarmBench-Response, SafeRLHF). Metrics reported are classification F1 scores, comparing against Qwen3Guard and YuFeng-XGuard baselines with parameter sizes from 0.6B to 8B.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies on Training Components
experiments.detail: Ablations isolate the effects of intent labels, CoT allocation strategies, hard-case supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO). Selective CoT on borderline samples yields the best average F1, confirming the importance of matching supervision to sample difficulty.

experiments.title: Model Size and Efficiency Comparison
experiments.detail: DT-Guard with a 4B backbone outperforms strong 8B guardrail baselines, demonstrating that reasoning supervision internalized during training can compensate for smaller model size while maintaining low-latency inference.

findings.title: Superior Safety Classification Performance
findings.detail: DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 on prompt-side and 0.870 on response-side safety benchmarks, outperforming Qwen3Guard-8B (0.852 prompt-side) and YuFeng-XGuard-8B baselines.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Intent Labels
findings.detail: Adding intent supervision improves prompt-side average F1 from 0.855 to 0.863, indicating that modeling interaction motivation aids in disambiguating semantically similar but safety-divergent requests.

findings.title: Selective CoT Training Improves Robustness
findings.detail: Applying chain-of-thought supervision only to borderline samples increases average F1 to 0.860, whereas full CoT training reduces performance to 0.828 due to format mismatch with reasoning-free inference.

findings.title: RG-PHO Enhances Hard-Case Handling
findings.detail: Multi-rollout consistency stratification enables targeted optimization of persistently failed and preference-unstable samples, improving model stability and judgment quality on difficult cases.

findings.title: Efficiency Gains from Reasoning-Free Inference
findings.detail: By emitting only structured safety labels at inference, DT-Guard avoids token-generation overhead of reasoning chains, enabling deployment in low-latency, high-throughput industrial systems.

contributions: Proposed DT-Guard, a safety guardrail model combining reasoning-active training with reasoning-free inference for efficient and robust safety judgment.
Formulated safety judgment as a progressive Intent → Category → Safety decision process with intent-driven dataset construction.
Introduced Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization to stratify and optimize hard safety cases via multi-rollout consistency.
Demonstrated that reasoning supervision can be internalized to outperform larger guardrail models with smaller backbones under low-latency inference constraints.
limitations: Lack of detailed failure mode analysis or error case studies limits understanding of residual risks.
Generalization to unseen or evolving safety risks beyond benchmark datasets is not evaluated.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical guarantees are provided for the rollout consistency stratification approach.
The impact of model architecture variations or larger-scale training data on DT-Guard performance is not explored.
open_questions: How well does DT-Guard generalize to novel or adversarially crafted safety risks outside the training distribution?
Can rollout-guided hard-case optimization be extended or formalized with theoretical guarantees for safety-critical applications?
What are the trade-offs between reasoning supervision granularity and inference efficiency in other safety-critical LLM tasks?
How does DT-Guard perform when integrated with larger backbone models or multimodal inputs?

papers.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
papers.abstract: As available training data approaches its physical limit, gains from Scaling Laws have begun to diminish. Consequently, improving Large Language Models (LLMs) now depends less on data expansion and more on higher-quality data utilization. However, in the context of large-scale corpora, existing refinement methodologies face significant limitations in quality, efficiency, and reliability: Rule-based approaches are constrained by fixed heuristics and struggle with instance-level variations; LLM-based approaches improve quality but fail to meet the efficiency and reliability requirements of large-scale data processing. To address these challenges, we propose UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework for large-scale pre-training data that completes the editing function space by introducing insertion in addition to deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level editing. Specifically, UltraX builds a reliable program-supervision generation pipeline. In this pipeline, dataset-adaptive prompt optimization first guides an expert LLM to produce high-quality end-to-end refined texts, and Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement then convert original-refined text pairs into structured program supervision. Meanwhile, UltraX improves supervision quality and stabilizes the training distribution with low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination. During inference and execution, it normalizes and validates model outputs through sliding-window prediction, global operation aggregation, and systematic post-processing, improving the stability and reliability of large-scale execution. Experiments show that UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all corpora and also matches or surpasses baselines with fewer training tokens, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability.

summary.takeaway: UltraX introduces a function-calling refinement framework with insertion, deletion, and modification operations, achieving superior data refinement quality and efficiency for large-scale LLM pre-training.
summary.problem: Existing large-scale pre-training data refinement methods either lack fine-grained editing capabilities or fail to scale efficiently and reliably to massive corpora.
summary.method: UltraX constructs a program-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, dynamic context replacement, and robust execution with sliding-window prediction and post-processing.
summary.evidence: Experiments with 1B parameter models pretrained on multiple corpora show UltraX surpasses baselines by over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets while using fewer training tokens.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UltraX’s performance on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation nor does it address potential biases inherited from expert LLMs used in supervision generation.
summary.why_for_you: UltraX offers a scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement approach that improves pre-training data quality and efficiency, directly addressing challenges in trustworthy and efficient LLM data utilization.

signals.text: UltraX achieves over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets in downstream tasks using 1B parameter models pretrained from scratch, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability compared to baselines.

UltraX’s program-supervision pipeline includes dataset-adaptive prompt optimization guiding an expert LLM to generate high-quality refined texts, followed by line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement to convert text pairs into structured editing programs.

UltraX stabilizes training distribution and improves supervision quality via low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination, while inference uses sliding-window prediction and global operation aggregation to ensure stable large-scale execution.

deep_dive.overview: UltraX addresses the diminishing returns of scaling LLM training data by focusing on improving data quality through fine-grained, programmatic editing of pre-training corpora. Unlike prior rule-based or LLM-based refinement methods limited by fixed heuristics or computational inefficiency, UltraX completes the editing function space by adding insertion to deletion and modification, enabling nuanced instance-level edits. It constructs a reliable program supervision pipeline where an expert LLM, guided by dataset-adaptive prompts, produces end-to-end refined texts. These are converted into structured editing operations via line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement. To ensure training stability and quality, UltraX filters low-confidence examples and controls sampling ratios of operation types. During inference, it segments long documents with sliding windows, predicts local operations, aggregates them globally, and applies systematic post-processing to produce stable, executable refinement programs. Experiments with 1B models pretrained on multiple corpora demonstrate UltraX’s superior average performance and data efficiency, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on several datasets, validating its approach to scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement for LLM pre-training.

methodology.title: Dataset-Adaptive Prompt Optimization
methodology.detail: UltraX first optimizes prompts tailored to each dataset to guide an expert LLM in generating high-quality, end-to-end refined texts from raw inputs, ensuring that the refinement captures dataset-specific nuances and semantic improvements.

methodology.title: Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement
methodology.detail: These techniques convert original and refined text pairs into structured program supervision by aligning lines between versions and replacing context dynamically, enabling the extraction of precise editing operations such as insertion, deletion, and modification.

methodology.title: Low-Confidence Example Filtering and Ratio-Controlled Sampling
methodology.detail: To improve supervision quality and stabilize training, UltraX filters out examples with low confidence scores and controls the sampling ratio of different operation combinations, balancing the training distribution across insertion, deletion, and modification operations.

methodology.title: Sliding-Window Segment-wise Operation Prediction
methodology.detail: During inference, UltraX segments long documents using a sliding-window approach, normalizes line numbers, and independently predicts editing operation sequences for each segment to handle length constraints and maintain local context.

methodology.title: Global Operation Aggregation and Systematic Post-Processing
methodology.detail: Local operation sequences from segments are merged into a global program by mapping operations to global line numbers, filtering duplicates, merging adjacent or interfering operations, and applying fallback mechanisms to ensure stable, executable refinement programs.

mechanism.title: Programmatic Editing with Complete Operation Space
mechanism.detail: UltraX extends the editing function space by including insertion alongside deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level edits that preserve semantic coherence and restore missing information, overcoming limitations of prior deletion-only or replacement-only frameworks.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes a deterministic function executor that applies predicted editing operations to original texts, ensuring auditable and interpretable refinement.

experiments.title: Pretraining 1B Parameter Models on Multiple Corpora
experiments.detail: UltraX was evaluated by pretraining 1B parameter language models from scratch on multiple large-scale corpora, comparing downstream task performance against baselines including raw data and ProX refinement, measuring average accuracy improvements and data efficiency.

experiments.title: Downstream Task Evaluation Across Ten Tasks
experiments.detail: Performance was assessed on ten downstream tasks including ARC-C, ARC-E, CSQA, HellaS, MMLU, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoG, and SciQ, with varying numbers of training tokens, demonstrating consistent gains and surpassing baselines with fewer tokens.

experiments.title: Ablation on Operation Combination Sampling
experiments.detail: The effect of ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination was analyzed to understand its impact on training stability and refinement quality, showing that balanced sampling improves model performance.

findings.title: Superior Average Performance
findings.detail: UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all evaluated corpora, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on multiple datasets compared to baseline methods.

findings.title: Improved Data Efficiency
findings.detail: UltraX matches or surpasses baseline refinement methods while using fewer training tokens, indicating stronger data efficiency in pre-training.

findings.title: Fine-Grained Refinement Balances Noise Removal and Preservation
findings.detail: Analyses suggest UltraX’s inclusion of insertion operations alongside deletion and modification enables better balance between removing noise and preserving useful information, reducing semantic fragmentation.

findings.title: Stable Large-Scale Execution
findings.detail: The sliding-window prediction, global aggregation, and systematic post-processing pipeline improve the stability and reliability of large-scale data refinement execution.

contributions: Proposed UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework introducing insertion to complete the editing function space for fine-grained instance-level editing.
Developed a reliable seed-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, and dynamic context replacement to generate structured program supervision.
Designed a robust large-scale execution pipeline with systematic post-processing to handle duplicate matching, ambiguous replacements, and operation interference.
Demonstrated consistent downstream performance improvements and stronger data efficiency across multiple large-scale pre-training corpora.
limitations: Lack of detailed evaluation on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation and its impact on refinement quality.
Potential biases and errors inherited from expert LLMs used in generating seed supervision are not explicitly analyzed.
No formal theoretical or causal mechanism is provided to explain the editing operation interactions or their effect on model performance.
Limited discussion on the computational cost and scalability trade-offs compared to other LLM-based refinement methods.
open_questions: How does UltraX perform on extremely long documents or streaming data beyond the sliding-window segmentation approach?
What are the effects of expert LLM biases on the quality and reliability of generated program supervision?
Can the programmatic editing framework be extended to incorporate semantic or syntactic constraints to further improve refinement quality?
How does UltraX compare in computational efficiency and cost to other state-of-the-art LLM-based refinement methods at larger model scales?

papers.title: WordVoice: Explicit and Decoupled Multi-Dimensional Word-Level Control for LLM-Based TTS
papers.abstract: While recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems have achieved remarkable naturalness, they predominantly rely on implicit end-to-end generation paradigms, resulting in coarse-grained control. In scenarios demanding precise stylistic interventions and strict temporal alignment, such as audiobook narration and video dubbing, the inability to explicitly manipulate word-level acoustic attributes remains a critical bottleneck. This limitation is primarily amplified by the severe scarcity of fine-grained annotated datasets and the architectural challenge of integrating multi-dimensional control signals into discrete autoregressive generation. To address this, we propose a unified framework for highly precise word-level control. First, we construct WordVoice-5A, a massive 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset featuring five-dimensional word-level annotations (duration, boundary, energy, pitch and tone) developed through a rigorous linguistically-guided pipeline. Second, we introduce WordVoice to transform the implicit generation process into an explicit, highly controllable paradigm. Specifically, we introduce a bound-token mechanism within the LLM to formulate an explicit ``acoustic planning'' process, enabling adaptive multi-task prosodic planning and flexible manual intervention. Furthermore, we augment the token-to-waveform stage with a fine-grained acoustic modulation module, bridging the resolution gap to strictly align word-level attributes between highly compressed discrete tokens and continuous waveforms. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WordVoice achieves superior, decoupled control over multiple acoustic dimensions while maintaining competitive zero-shot synthesis stability. The code and audio samples are publicly available at https://xxh333.github.io/wordvoice-demo/.

summary.takeaway: WordVoice introduces explicit, multi-dimensional word-level control in LLM-based TTS, achieving precise prosodic manipulation and strict temporal alignment.
summary.problem: Current LLM-based TTS systems lack fine-grained, explicit control over multiple acoustic attributes at the word level, limiting applications requiring precise stylistic and temporal adjustments.
summary.method: WordVoice combines a large-scale, linguistically annotated dataset (WordVoice-5A) with an explicit bound-token acoustic planning mechanism in the LLM and a fine-grained acoustic modulation module in the token-to-waveform stage.
summary.evidence: Experiments on a 4.7k-hour bilingual test set show WordVoice outperforms baselines like CosyVoice3 in controllability (Ctrl-MOS) and naturalness (N-MOS), with objective metrics confirming superior multi-attribute alignment and temporal precision.
summary.limitations: Tone control remains partially entangled with other acoustic features due to its dynamic nature, and strong localized prosodic variations slightly reduce speaker similarity.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a novel, data-driven framework and architectural design enabling explicit, decoupled multi-dimensional word-level control in LLM-based TTS, advancing trustworthy and precise prosodic synthesis.

signals.text: WordVoice-5A is a 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset with five-dimensional word-level annotations (duration, boundary, energy, pitch, tone), enabling supervised training for explicit multi-attribute control.

The bound-token mechanism restructures the LLM’s autoregressive generation to explicitly plan acoustic attributes before speech token generation, allowing adaptive multi-task prosodic planning and manual intervention.
Objective evaluations show WordVoice reduces duration mean absolute error (Dur-MAE) and boundary error rate (Bnd-ER) compared to MagicTTS, demonstrating improved temporal alignment precision.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical limitation of coarse-grained control in current LLM-based TTS systems by proposing WordVoice, a framework enabling explicit, multi-dimensional word-level control. The authors first construct WordVoice-5A, a large-scale bilingual dataset with detailed word-level acoustic annotations across five dimensions. Leveraging this data, WordVoice introduces a novel bound-token mechanism within the LLM to explicitly plan acoustic attributes in an autoregressive manner, enabling both autonomous prosodic generation and manual attribute specification. To bridge the resolution gap between discrete tokens and continuous waveforms, a fine-grained acoustic modulation module is integrated into the token-to-waveform stage. Extensive experiments on unseen Chinese and English utterances demonstrate that WordVoice achieves superior controllability and naturalness compared to strong baselines, validated by subjective MOS tests and objective acoustic metrics. Ablation studies confirm the decoupling of acoustic attributes and the necessity of the modulation module for detailed acoustic reconstruction. The work significantly advances precise prosodic control in TTS, crucial for applications like audiobook narration and video dubbing requiring strict temporal and stylistic fidelity.

methodology.title: WordVoice-5A Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: A linguistically-guided annotation pipeline produces a 4.7k-hour bilingual dataset with five word-level acoustic attributes: duration, boundary, energy, pitch, and tone. This dataset supports supervised training for explicit multi-dimensional control.

methodology.title: Bound-Token Acoustic Planning Mechanism
methodology.detail: Within the autoregressive LLM, special bound-tokens explicitly represent acoustic attributes, enabling the model to plan prosody before generating speech tokens. This restructures generation from implicit to explicit, allowing adaptive multi-task control and manual intervention.

methodology.title: Fine-Grained Acoustic Modulation Module
methodology.detail: Inserted in the token-to-waveform stage, this module compensates for acoustic details lost during discrete token quantization by modulating continuous waveforms with word-level style tokens, ensuring strict alignment of acoustic attributes.

methodology.title: Training Objectives
methodology.detail: The LLM is trained to predict acoustic attributes and speech tokens autoregressively, while the modulation module uses a Flow Matching objective to reconstruct acoustic details, with random masking of speech tokens to enforce reliance on style conditions.

mechanism.title: Acoustic Planning via Bound-Tokens
mechanism.detail: The bound-token mechanism explicitly encodes word-level acoustic attributes within the LLM’s autoregressive generation, enabling causal reasoning about prosodic execution prior to speech token generation. This explicit planning contrasts with implicit end-to-end generation, facilitating decoupled multi-dimensional control.

mechanism.title: No Additional Mechanistic Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide explicit equations or causal models beyond the description of the bound-token mechanism and Flow Matching loss.

experiments.title: Subjective Evaluation on WordVoice-5A Test Set
experiments.detail: Crowd-sourced listening tests with 20 participants rated 80 utterances per model on naturalness (N-MOS), speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), and word style control (Ctrl-MOS). WordVoice-Control achieved statistically significant improvements in controllability and naturalness over CosyVoice3.

experiments.title: Objective Acoustic Attribute Evaluation
experiments.detail: Metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER), Duration Mean Absolute Error (Dur-MAE), Energy MAE, Pitch MAE, Boundary Error Rate (Bnd-ER), and Tone Relative Error Rate (Ton-RER) were computed on Chinese and English test sets, showing WordVoice variants outperform baselines and ablations.

experiments.title: Temporal Control Precision Comparison
experiments.detail: WordVoice demonstrated lower Dur-MAE and Bnd-ER than MagicTTS variants on both Chinese and English test sets, confirming superior explicit temporal alignment.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies on Attribute Decoupling and Modulation Module
experiments.detail: Single-attribute control experiments confirmed decoupling of duration, boundary, energy, and pitch, with tone showing partial entanglement. Removing the modulation module degraded energy and pitch reconstruction, validating its role in acoustic detail compensation.

findings.title: Superior Multi-Dimensional Control
findings.detail: WordVoice achieves explicit, decoupled control over duration, boundary, energy, pitch, and tone at the word level, outperforming prior methods limited to unidimensional or implicit control.

findings.title: Improved Naturalness and Controllability
findings.detail: WordVoice-Control variant significantly improves naturalness (N-MOS) and word-level style control (Ctrl-MOS) over CosyVoice3, with p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively, demonstrating effective prosodic planning.

findings.title: Tradeoff in Speaker Similarity
findings.detail: Localized prosodic variations introduced by WordVoice cause minor reductions in speaker similarity (Spk-MOS), reflecting a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.

findings.title: Temporal Alignment Precision
findings.detail: WordVoice reduces duration MAE and boundary error rates compared to MagicTTS, confirming more precise explicit temporal control.

findings.title: Necessity of Acoustic Modulation Module
findings.detail: Ablations show that removing the WordVoice-FM module significantly degrades energy and pitch reconstruction, confirming its critical role in restoring acoustic details lost in token quantization.

contributions: Construction and open-sourcing of WordVoice-5A, a large-scale bilingual dataset with five-dimensional word-level acoustic annotations.
Introduction of the bound-token mechanism enabling explicit acoustic planning within an autoregressive LLM for multi-dimensional prosodic control.
Development of a fine-grained acoustic modulation module bridging discrete token representations and continuous waveform synthesis.
Comprehensive evaluation demonstrating superior word-level control, naturalness, and temporal alignment over state-of-the-art baselines.
limitations: Tone attribute control is only partially decoupled due to its dynamic variation nature, complicating absolute disentanglement from other acoustic features.
Strong localized prosodic manipulations slightly reduce speaker similarity, indicating a tradeoff between expressiveness and timbre consistency.
The approach relies on a large-scale annotated dataset, which may limit applicability in low-resource languages or domains without such data.
No explicit mechanistic or theoretical modeling beyond architectural design and loss functions is provided.
open_questions: How can tone control be further disentangled from other acoustic attributes to achieve fully independent manipulation?
Can the WordVoice framework be adapted or extended to low-resource languages lacking large-scale annotated datasets?
What are the impacts of explicit multi-dimensional control on downstream tasks such as emotion recognition or speaker adaptation?
How does the tradeoff between localized prosodic expressiveness and speaker similarity affect user acceptance in real-world applications?

papers.title: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
papers.abstract: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q\&A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings.

summary.takeaway: The study reveals that reasoning in English significantly enhances uncertainty estimation (UE) performance across multiple languages.
summary.problem: Existing research on uncertainty estimation has primarily focused on English, neglecting multilingual contexts.
summary.method: The authors evaluate nine UE methods across 22 languages using two human-curated Q&A datasets.
summary.evidence: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages improves UE performance, closing the gap between resource levels.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to two MCQA datasets, which may not fully capture the diversity of real-world NLP applications.
summary.why_for_you: This research is crucial for developing trustworthy LLMs capable of effective multilingual uncertainty estimation.

signals.text: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages significantly improves UE performance, indicating that comprehension is intact but generation is the bottleneck.
The study evaluates nine UE methods, including open-box methods like Token Entropy and closed-box methods like Self Verbalized uncertainty, across various model sizes.
The closed-box Self Verbalized method achieves an average AUROC of 0.72, outperforming other methods, particularly in high-resource languages.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the gap in uncertainty estimation (UE) methods for multilingual large language models (LLMs), focusing on the performance of nine UE methods across 22 languages. The study finds that reasoning in English while using low-resource languages enhances UE performance, suggesting that generation language is more critical than question language. The results indicate that the choice of UE method should be model-scale dependent, with open-box methods performing better at smaller scales and closed-box methods excelling at larger scales. This comprehensive evaluation provides actionable insights for improving multilingual LLM reliability.

methodology.title: Open-Box Methods
methodology.detail: These methods utilize internal model representations to derive uncertainty, including Token Entropy and Maximum-Sequence-Probability, which aggregate token-level logits into sequence-level scores.

methodology.title: Closed-Box Methods
methodology.detail: Closed-box techniques, such as Self Verbalized uncertainty, rely solely on generated text, prompting the model to express its confidence, although they may struggle with calibration.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The study employs exact matching against human-curated labels for evaluation, avoiding automated ground truth matching to reduce noise and bias in UE performance assessment.

methodology.title: Data Sources
methodology.detail: Two human-curated Q&A datasets are used, covering high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, ensuring a diverse representation of linguistic contexts.

mechanism.title: Uncertainty Estimation Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The study does not provide a specific mechanism for how uncertainty is estimated but categorizes methods into open-box and closed-box approaches based on model access.

experiments.title: Evaluation of UE Methods
experiments.detail: Nine UE methods are evaluated across 22 languages using two models, Gemma327B and Qwen3-235B, with performance measured by AUROC.

experiments.title: Impact of Reasoning Language
experiments.detail: The experiments demonstrate that reasoning in English while using low-resource languages significantly improves UE performance, with the Self Verbalized method achieving an AUROC of 0.72.

experiments.title: Model Scaling Effects
experiments.detail: The study analyzes how UE performance varies with model scale, showing that open-box methods outperform at smaller scales while closed-box methods excel at larger scales.

findings.title: Improved UE with English Reasoning
findings.detail: Prompting models to reason in English while using low-resource languages improves UE performance, indicating a generation bottleneck.

findings.title: Language Generation Matters
findings.detail: The performance gap in UE between low and high-resource languages is closed when models reason in English, highlighting the importance of generation language.

findings.title: Model Scale Dependency
findings.detail: At smaller model scales, open-box methods like Token Entropy outperform closed-box methods, while at larger scales, closed-box methods like Self Verbalized uncertainty become superior.

contributions: First large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages.
Identification of the importance of reasoning language over question language in UE performance.
Guidance on selecting UE methods based on model scale.
limitations: Focus on only two MCQA datasets may not represent the full diversity of NLP applications.
Exclusion of training-based UE methods limits the scope of the analysis.
open_questions: How can UE methods be further improved for low-resource languages?
What are the implications of different UE methods in real-world applications?

papers.title: Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier? Benchmarking Rubric LLMs for Deep-Research Source Attribution
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning increasingly relies on an LLM judge to score each rubric criterion, and that judge acts as the reward model during training. Before such a signal can be trusted, we need to know how capable the judge must be and how biased it is. We study this calibration question for citation quality in deep-research systems, where a search-grounded LLM must support each claim it writes with a cited source. Citation quality is a structured rubric task in which each attribution-citation pair is judged along two dimensions that require an LLM, source relevance and factual support. On an adversarial long-form benchmark, we score 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families against gold labels over 1,248 rubric decisions, all of which were human-reviewed and 378 of which were hard cases adjudicated from judge disagreements. Cheaper judges remain competitive across both dimensions, with GPT-5-mini attaining the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 ($κ$=0.636), while on factual support the judges are statistically indistinguishable (overlapping confidence intervals), so no single model dominates. At comparable F1, the judges still differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Scalar F1 obscures this directional bias, yet it is exactly what a downstream reinforcement learning loop would reinforce. Calibrating the judge is therefore a prerequisite for using citation rubrics as reward signals, and our results show that this calibration does not require the most expensive available model.

summary.takeaway: Cheaper off-the-shelf LLM judges can reliably evaluate citation quality for source relevance and factual support without requiring the most expensive frontier models.
summary.problem: Determining how capable and unbiased an LLM judge must be to serve as a trustworthy reward model for citation quality in deep-research systems.
summary.method: Benchmarking 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families on an adversarial long-form citation quality task with human-reviewed gold labels across source relevance and factual support dimensions.
summary.evidence: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 (κ=0.636), and judges were statistically indistinguishable on factual support, with detailed bias metrics revealing differences in pass-rate drift, false positive, and false negative rates.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide evidence on how judge calibration impacts downstream reinforcement learning training quality or explore mechanisms to correct directional biases in judges.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding judge calibration and bias in citation verification enables efficient and trustworthy reward modeling for RL training in deep-research LLM applications.

signals.text: GPT-5-mini attained the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 with Cohen’s κ=0.636, outperforming more expensive models on this dimension.
The evaluation framework uses a rubric with two LLM-judged criteria—source relevance and factual support—each scored binarily with rationale, enabling structured and interpretable judge assessments.

Despite comparable F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, indicating that scalar F1 metrics obscure directional biases critical for reinforcement learning reward signals.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the calibration of LLM judges used as reward models in reinforcement learning for citation quality in deep-research systems. The authors construct an adversarial benchmark spanning 25 diverse topics with 1,248 human-reviewed rubric decisions on source relevance and factual support. They evaluate 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families, measuring pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, and bias metrics such as pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Results show that smaller, cheaper models like GPT-5-mini can match or exceed the performance of larger frontier models on source relevance, while factual support judgments are statistically indistinguishable across judges. However, differences in directional bias metrics reveal that scalar accuracy metrics alone are insufficient to characterize judge reliability for downstream RL training. The study concludes that careful calibration of judges is essential but does not require the most expensive models, enabling more cost-effective and trustworthy citation verification in RL pipelines.

methodology.title: Benchmark Construction
methodology.detail: The Deep-Research Citation Benchmark includes 25 diverse topics with long-form summaries and adversarially edited claims using 19 strategies. Attribution-citation pairs are parsed and scored on three criteria: link accessibility (deterministic), source relevance, and factual support (both LLM-judged). A council of 6 LLM judges independently labels pairs, with human review validating all 1,248 decisions and adjudicating 378 hard cases.

methodology.title: Judge Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Judges produce binary pass/fail scores per criterion with free-text rationales. Metrics include pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ for agreement, pass-rate drift (judge vs. gold pass rate), false positive rate (accepting bad citations), and false negative rate (rejecting good citations). These metrics characterize both accuracy and directional bias relevant for RL reward signals.

methodology.title: Judge Models and Setup
methodology.detail: Eight LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families are evaluated via cloud inference APIs. Each judge scores all 624 source relevance and 624 factual support pairs. Two judges (GPT-5-mini and Claude Opus 4.6) also contributed to gold labels, enabling council-independent comparisons.

methodology.title: Prompt Design
methodology.detail: Prompts instruct judges to provide binary scores and rationales for source relevance and factual support, emphasizing expert evaluation criteria such as topical relevance, claim support, factual consistency, and contradiction detection. The same prompts are applied uniformly across all judges.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models explaining judge behavior or bias mechanisms, focusing instead on empirical benchmarking and metric analysis.

experiments.title: Adversarial Long-Form Citation Benchmark
experiments.detail: The benchmark contains 1,248 rubric decisions over 624 attribution-citation pairs, with 378 hard cases adjudicated by humans. Judges are evaluated on source relevance and factual support dimensions using pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate.

experiments.title: Judge Cost-Quality Tradeoff Analysis
experiments.detail: The study compares judge accuracy metrics against estimated cost per decision on a logarithmic scale, showing that cheaper judges like GPT-5-mini achieve competitive or superior performance relative to more expensive models.

findings.title: Cheaper Judges Competitive on Source Relevance
findings.detail: GPT-5-mini achieves the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 and Cohen’s κ of 0.636, outperforming larger models, demonstrating that smaller judges can reliably assess topical relevance.

findings.title: No Single Judge Dominates Factual Support
findings.detail: On factual support, judges’ performance overlaps within confidence intervals, indicating no statistically significant difference in accuracy among the evaluated models.

findings.title: Directional Biases Vary Across Judges
findings.detail: Despite similar F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, revealing biases that scalar metrics like F1 fail to capture but that affect RL reward signals.

contributions: Introduces a large adversarial benchmark for citation quality evaluation with human-reviewed gold labels across diverse topics.
Comprehensively evaluates 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges on source relevance and factual support, including bias metrics critical for RL reward modeling.
Demonstrates that smaller, cheaper LLM judges can match or exceed frontier models in citation verification tasks.
Highlights the importance of calibrating judges to account for directional biases that scalar accuracy metrics obscure.
limitations: Does not analyze the impact of judge calibration on downstream reinforcement learning training outcomes.
Lacks exploration of methods to mitigate or correct directional biases in judge models.
No mechanistic or theoretical explanation is provided for observed judge biases or performance differences.
Evaluation is limited to off-the-shelf models accessed via APIs, without fine-tuning or adaptation experiments.
open_questions: How do directional biases in LLM judges affect the stability and quality of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards?
What calibration or debiasing techniques can effectively reduce false positive and false negative rates in LLM judges?
Can smaller LLM judges be fine-tuned or adapted to further close gaps in factual support evaluation?
How does retrieval quality interact with judge performance and bias in citation verification pipelines?

papers.title: When the Judge Changes, So Does the Measurement: Auditing LLM-as-Judge Reliability
papers.abstract: An LLM-as-judge score can move even when the candidate responses stay fixed, simply because the evaluator has changed. We treat this evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem. Across four judgment datasets, we compare two upgrade paths available in practice: scaling Qwen3 dense judges from 1.7B to 32B parameters and moving across MiniMax M2-M2.7 released APIs. The main pattern is that judge upgrades are not interchangeable: only Qwen3 1.7B to 4B gives a robust adjacent gain, while MiniMax adjacent releases do not. Stronger judges reduce but do not remove position and verbosity bias. Repeated-sample juries add little when errors are correlated. Structured debate can move decisions substantially, but without parser and fallback logs those shifts cannot be attributed to deliberation. We argue that LLM-as-judge reports should include dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.

summary.takeaway: LLM-as-judge reliability varies with evaluator changes, showing that judge upgrades are not interchangeable and that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases or correlated errors.
summary.problem: Replacing an LLM evaluator changes measured scores even with fixed candidate responses, creating evaluator-replacement ambiguity that challenges measurement validity.
summary.method: The study compares two evaluator upgrade paths—Qwen3 parameter scaling (1.7B to 32B) and MiniMax M2–M2.7 API releases—across four judgment datasets, analyzing accuracy, bias, error correlation, and protocol auditability.
summary.evidence: Empirical results show only Qwen3 1.7B→4B scaling yields robust adjacent gains, MiniMax releases lack consistent gains, stronger judges reduce position and verbosity bias but do not remove them, and jury aggregation gains are limited by high error correlation.
summary.limitations: The study does not establish causal claims about MiniMax internals and lacks parser and fallback logs to fully attribute debate-induced decision shifts.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding evaluator-replacement ambiguity and multi-dimensional reliability components is critical for trustworthy LLM evaluation and designing robust LLM-as-judge protocols.

signals.text: Only the Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters produces a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability, while MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not yield consistent improvements across datasets.

The study operationalizes LLM-as-judge reliability into four components—judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability—measured via accuracy, Cohen’s κ, position flip rates, error correlation ρ, and parse status.
High intra-class error correlations (ρ up to 0.972 for Qwen3 juries) limit jury aggregation gains, as majority voting fails to amplify reliability when errors are dependent rather than independent.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the evaluator-replacement ambiguity in LLM-as-judge evaluation, where changing the evaluator model alters measured scores despite fixed candidate responses. It investigates whether improvements in judge reliability arise from increased evaluator capability or other factors like bias and protocol design. The authors compare two upgrade paths: parameter scaling of Qwen3 judges (1.7B to 32B parameters) and released-model upgrades of MiniMax M2 to M2.7 APIs, across four diverse judgment datasets. They decompose reliability into four operational components—accuracy, bias robustness, error correlation, and auditability—and analyze how these interact with evaluator scaling and aggregation protocols. Results show that only Qwen3 scaling from 1.7B to 4B yields robust gains, while MiniMax upgrades do not consistently improve reliability. Stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate position and verbosity biases. Jury aggregation gains are limited by high correlated errors, and debate protocols require audit trails to attribute decision shifts properly. The study advocates for comprehensive reporting standards including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol logs to improve measurement validity in LLM-as-judge evaluations.

methodology.title: Evaluator Upgrade Comparison
methodology.detail: Two evaluator upgrade paths are compared: Qwen3 dense judges scaled from 1.7B to 32B parameters, and MiniMax M2 to M2.7 released APIs. This comparison isolates parameter scaling effects from released-model changes without causal claims about MiniMax internals.

methodology.title: Reliability Operationalization
methodology.detail: LLM-as-judge reliability is decomposed into four constructs: judgment validity (accuracy, Cohen’s κ, Spearman correlation), bias robustness (position flip, verbosity bias, granularity sensitivity), aggregation independence (error correlation ρ, jury gain), and protocol auditability (parse status, fallback behavior, intermediate verdicts).

methodology.title: Datasets and Judges
methodology.detail: Eight judges (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 14B, 32B; MiniMax M2, M2.1, M2.5, M2.7) are evaluated on four datasets: LLMBar (419 adversarial pairs), PandaLM testset-v1 (894 pairwise examples), Chatbot Arena seed-42 (1,997 pairwise examples), and Judge’s Verdict (200 TechQA-derived examples with pointwise labels).

methodology.title: Aggregation and Debate Protocols
methodology.detail: Jury aggregation experiments estimate intra-class error correlation ρ to assess independence assumptions. Debate experiments analyze decision shifts but highlight the need for parser and fallback logs to attribute changes to deliberation.

mechanism.title: Evaluator-Replacement Ambiguity
mechanism.detail: The paper conceptualizes the measurement pipeline as comprising candidate responses, benchmark slice, judge model, prompt/decoding, parser, and aggregation/debate. Changes in any component, especially the judge model, can alter reported scores, creating ambiguity about the source of score changes.

mechanism.title: Error Correlation and Jury Aggregation
mechanism.detail: High intra-class error correlation ρ among jurors violates independence assumptions of Condorcet-style majority voting, limiting jury accuracy gains. The beta-binomial model corrected by ρ accurately predicts jury accuracy, showing that correlated errors constrain aggregation benefits.

experiments.title: Judge Upgrade Evaluation
experiments.detail: Evaluated eight judges across four datasets using fixed main prompts. Metrics include accuracy, Cohen’s κ, and Spearman correlation. The study compares adjacent judge upgrades along parameter scaling and released-model axes to assess reliability gains.

experiments.title: Bias Probing
experiments.detail: Position-flip rates, verbosity bias, and granularity sensitivity are measured to assess bias robustness. Results show stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate these biases, with position-flip rates decreasing from 0.320 (Qwen3-1.7B) to 0.117–0.147 (MiniMax releases).

experiments.title: Jury Aggregation Experiment
experiments.detail: Homogeneous and heterogeneous juries are formed to test aggregation gains. Error correlation ρ is estimated from vote matrices, showing high correlation (up to 0.972) that limits majority voting improvements. Beta-binomial models corrected by ρ closely predict observed jury accuracy.

experiments.title: Debate Protocol Case Study
experiments.detail: Structured debate experiments reveal substantial decision shifts, but lack of parser and fallback logs prevents attribution of these shifts to deliberation, highlighting the need for audit trails in debate protocols.

findings.title: Non-Interchangeability of Judge Upgrades
findings.detail: Only Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters yields a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability; MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not show consistent improvements across datasets.

findings.title: Bias Reduction but Persistence
findings.detail: Stronger judges reduce position-flip rates from 0.320 to approximately 0.117–0.147 and verbosity bias from 0.547 to about 0.13, but biases remain nonzero, indicating capability improves but does not eliminate bias.

findings.title: Limited Jury Gains Due to Correlated Errors
findings.detail: High intra-class error correlations (ρ = 0.944–0.972 for Qwen3 juries) cause majority voting to yield minimal accuracy improvements, with jury size increases from 1 to 5 only marginally improving accuracy (e.g., 0.463 to 0.482 on LLMBar).

findings.title: Debate Shifts Require Audit Trails
findings.detail: Structured debate can substantially change decisions, but without parser and fallback logs, these shifts cannot be confidently attributed to deliberation processes.

findings.title: Dataset-Specific Evaluator Strength
findings.detail: No single judge dominates all datasets: GLM-5.1 leads on LLMBar, MiniMax-M2.7 leads on PandaLM, and mimo-v2-pro leads on Chatbot Arena, emphasizing slice-specific measurement validity.

contributions: Formulation of evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem in LLM-as-judge evaluation.
A two-axis empirical study comparing parameter scaling and released-model upgrades across multiple datasets and judges.
Decomposition of LLM-as-judge reliability into judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability.
Demonstration that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases and that jury aggregation gains are limited by correlated errors.
Proposal of a reporting standard including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.
limitations: No causal claims are made about MiniMax internal model changes due to lack of controlled ablation.
Absence of parser and fallback logs limits attribution of debate-induced decision shifts to actual deliberation.
Bias and reliability analyses are limited to the evaluated datasets and judge panels, restricting generalizability.
Prompt sensitivity is treated as a robustness check but not systematically explored, leaving prompt effects under-specified.
open_questions: How can audit trails be designed to reliably attribute decision shifts in multi-agent debate protocols?
What mechanisms underlie the persistence of bias despite increased evaluator capability?
Can error correlation among heterogeneous juries be reduced to improve aggregation gains?
How do prompt variations interact with evaluator scaling to affect measurement validity?

papers.title: From Voting to Agent Collaboration: Answer-Type-Aware LLM Pipelines for BioASQ 14b
papers.abstract: Biomedical question answering requires not only accurate extraction of information from scientific literature but also reliable integration of evidence across multiple documents. This study presents a question-type-specific large language model (LLM) framework for BioASQ 14b Task B, designed to improve answer robustness and evidence grounding in biomedical question answering. Rather than applying a single prompting strategy to all questions, the framework selects different inference procedures for yes/no, factoid, and list questions according to their distinct reasoning and evaluation requirements. For yes/no questions, snippet shuffling and self-reflection are used to reduce sensitivity to evidence ordering and improve decision stability. For factoid questions, full-snippet input is combined with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning to support accurate biomedical entity identification. For list questions, a multi-agent architecture is employed, in which evidence extraction, candidate generation, answer verification, and final aggregation are handled collaboratively. Preliminary experiments on BioASQ 13b were used to identify effective inference strategies for each question type, and the resulting framework was subsequently evaluated in the official BioASQ 14b Task B challenge. In the official evaluation, our framework showed competitive performance across multiple batches and achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining question-type-specific inference, ensemble prediction, and agent-based verification for reliable biomedical question answering.

summary.takeaway: The proposed LLM framework enhances biomedical question answering by tailoring inference strategies to specific question types.
summary.problem: Biomedical question answering faces challenges in accurately integrating evidence from diverse sources.
summary.method: The framework employs question-type-specific inference procedures, including snippet shuffling and multi-agent collaboration.
summary.evidence: In the BioASQ 14b Task B challenge, the framework achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4, demonstrating its effectiveness.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide detailed performance metrics for all question types across all batches.
summary.why_for_you: This research offers insights into improving LLM performance in specialized domains, relevant for trustworthy AI applications.

signals.text: The framework achieved a macro F1 score of 0.9110 for yes/no questions, indicating strong decision-making capabilities.
Utilizing a multi-agent architecture for list questions allows for collaborative evidence extraction and verification, enhancing answer reliability.
The use of snippet shuffling in yes/no questions reduced sensitivity to evidence ordering, improving decision stability and consistency.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the complexities of biomedical question answering by introducing a question-type-specific LLM framework for the BioASQ 14b Task B challenge. The framework adapts inference strategies for yes/no, factoid, and list questions, enhancing answer robustness and evidence grounding. Preliminary experiments on BioASQ 13b informed the selection of effective strategies, leading to competitive performance in the official evaluation, particularly achieving first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4. This demonstrates the potential of tailored inference methods in improving LLM capabilities in biomedical contexts.

methodology.title: Yes/No Question Processing
methodology.detail: The yes/no subsystem employs snippet shuffling and self-reflection to enhance decision stability. It utilizes an ensemble of four LLM configurations, querying each with varied snippet orders and aggregating results through majority voting.

methodology.title: Factoid Question Processing
methodology.detail: For factoid questions, the framework combines full-snippet input with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning to accurately identify biomedical entities, ensuring precise responses.

methodology.title: List Question Processing
methodology.detail: A multi-agent architecture is implemented for list questions, where evidence extraction, candidate generation, and answer verification are conducted collaboratively, improving overall answer quality.

mechanism.title: Ensemble Voting Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The yes/no subsystem utilizes a majority voting mechanism among multiple LLM outputs, with a verification agent employed when outputs conflict, ensuring robust decision-making.

experiments.title: BioASQ 13b Development Benchmark
experiments.detail: Preliminary experiments on the BioASQ 13b test set were conducted to evaluate various prompting strategies and model configurations, informing the final system design for BioASQ 14b.

experiments.title: Official BioASQ 14b Evaluation
experiments.detail: The framework was evaluated across four batches in the BioASQ 14b challenge, achieving an average score of 0.9110 for yes/no macro F1 and first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4.

findings.title: Performance in Yes/No Questions
findings.detail: The framework achieved a macro F1 score of 0.9110 for yes/no questions, indicating effective handling of binary decisions.

findings.title: Factoid Question Success
findings.detail: The system ranked first in the factoid subtask of Batch 4, demonstrating superior performance in identifying specific biomedical entities.

findings.title: List Question Challenges
findings.detail: The multi-agent architecture for list questions improved evidence integration, although specific performance metrics for this category were not detailed.

contributions: Introduction of a question-type-specific LLM framework for biomedical question answering.
Demonstration of effective ensemble strategies for improving answer robustness.
Implementation of a multi-agent architecture for collaborative evidence processing.
limitations: Lack of detailed performance metrics for list questions across all batches.
No comprehensive analysis of the impact of individual LLM configurations on overall performance.
open_questions: How can the framework be adapted for other domains beyond biomedical question answering?
What are the implications of varying LLM configurations on performance across different question types?

papers.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a powerful recipe for improving language-model reasoning, but it is expensive to repeat on every new strong model because the target model must generate many rollouts during training. As models scale, post-training itself becomes a bottleneck. We study a weak-to-strong alternative: run RL on a smaller model where rollouts are cheaper, then reuse what that RL run learned to improve a stronger target model. Directly distilling the post-RL weak teacher is not enough, because the teacher's final policy mixes useful RL gains with the limitations of the smaller model. We propose Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD), which transfers the teacher's RL-induced policy shift instead. Direct-OPD compares the post-RL teacher with its own pre-RL reference and treats their log-ratio as a dense implicit reward for the student. In plain terms, the checkpoint pair tells us which actions RL made the weak model more or less likely to take, and Direct-OPD applies that signal on the stronger student's own on-policy states. This directly reuses the weak model's RL supervision signal without training an explicit reward model or running sparse-reward RL on the target model. Empirically, Direct-OPD consistently leverages weaker teachers to improve stronger target models; notably, it boosts Qwen3-1.7B from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024 in just 4 hours on 8 A100 GPUs. It outperforms step-matched direct RL and enables the sequential composition of multiple policy shifts. Our results show that RL outcomes can be reused across model scales as implicit reward signals, not merely as final models to imitate.

summary.takeaway: Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) effectively enhances stronger language models by leveraging the policy shifts from weaker models trained with reinforcement learning.
summary.problem: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is computationally expensive for large models, creating a bottleneck in post-training.
summary.method: Direct-OPD transfers the RL-induced policy shift from a weaker model to a stronger model, treating the log-ratio of their policies as an implicit reward.
summary.evidence: Direct-OPD improved the Qwen3-1.7B model's performance from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024 in just 4 hours using 8 A100 GPUs.
summary.limitations: The effectiveness of Direct-OPD is conditional on the meaningfulness of the teacher/reference improvement on student-visited states.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides insights into efficient model training strategies, relevant for those focused on on-policy distillation and statistical theory for LLMs.

signals.text: Direct-OPD enables the transfer of RL-induced policy shifts rather than the final policy of the teacher, allowing stronger models to benefit from weaker ones without direct imitation.
The method utilizes the log-ratio of the post-RL teacher's policy against its pre-RL reference as a dense implicit reward, circumventing the need for an explicit reward model.
Empirical results demonstrate that Direct-OPD consistently improves stronger models across various teacher pairs and student families, indicating its robustness and generalizability.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of costly reinforcement learning (RL) processes in training large language models by proposing Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD). This method allows for the efficient transfer of RL-induced policy shifts from a weaker model to a stronger one, effectively reusing the RL supervision signal without the need for extensive rollouts on the target model. The strongest evidence supporting this approach is the significant performance boost of the Qwen3-1.7B model, which increased from 48.3% to 62.4% accuracy on AIME 2024 in a short training period, showcasing the potential of Direct-OPD in enhancing model capabilities while reducing computational costs.

methodology.title: Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD)
methodology.detail: Direct-OPD involves running RL on a smaller, cheaper model and transferring the learned policy shift to a stronger model. The method compares the post-RL teacher's policy with its pre-RL reference, using their log-ratio as an implicit reward for the student.

methodology.title: Policy Shift Transfer
methodology.detail: The transfer process focuses on the behavioral changes induced by the RL training of the weak model, rather than attempting to replicate the weak model's final policy, ensuring that stronger models can leverage useful RL insights.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: The evaluation of model performance is conducted using the AIME benchmarks, with specific metrics such as accuracy averaged over multiple samples to assess the effectiveness of the Direct-OPD approach.

mechanism.title: Policy-as-Reward Identity
mechanism.detail: Direct-OPD leverages the policy-as-reward identity, where the log-ratio of policies under KL-regularized RL can recover the reward signal, allowing for effective transfer of learned behaviors.

experiments.title: Improvement of Stronger Students
experiments.detail: In experiments, the policy shift from R1-Distill-1.5B to JustRL-1.5B was transferred to stronger models like R1-Distill-7B and Qwen3-4B, showing consistent performance improvements across different model families.

experiments.title: Comparison with Direct RL
experiments.detail: Direct-OPD was compared against step-matched direct RL, demonstrating superior performance in both accuracy and computational efficiency, validating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

experiments.title: Sequential Composition of Policy Shifts
experiments.detail: The ability to compose multiple independently learned policy shifts was tested, confirming that Direct-OPD can accumulate gains in a single student model, enhancing its overall performance.

findings.title: Effective Transfer Across Models
findings.detail: Direct-OPD successfully improved the performance of stronger models, such as Qwen3-1.7B, by utilizing policy shifts from weaker models, demonstrating the method's versatility.

findings.title: Significant Performance Gains
findings.detail: The Qwen3-1.7B model achieved a notable accuracy increase from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024, showcasing the practical benefits of Direct-OPD.

findings.title: Generalizability of Direct-OPD
findings.detail: The method proved effective across various teacher pairs and student families, indicating that Direct-OPD is not limited to specific model architectures or training data.

contributions: Introduction of Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) as a novel approach for weak-to-strong model training.
Demonstration of the effectiveness of transferring RL-induced policy shifts rather than final policies.
Empirical validation of Direct-OPD's performance improvements across different model families and training setups.
limitations: The signal's effectiveness is conditional on the meaningfulness of the teacher/reference improvement on student-visited states.
The best response length and KL strength remain dependent on the specific teacher-student pair.
open_questions: How can the conditional nature of the signal be mitigated to ensure consistent performance across all model pairs?
What are the optimal configurations for KL strength and response length in various training scenarios?
